                 INTRODUCTION.




I N this volume is continued the Roll or Register

of Burgesses and Guild-brethren of the City of

Edinburgh from 1st January 1701 to 31st December

1760.   Illustrative notes, glossary, etc., will be found

at the end of the volume.

       N O T E S O N BURGESS R O L L , 1701-1760.

    The dates quoted in the Burgess Roll of the admission of a burgess or
guild brother by the Town Council are frequently incorrect, and sometimes
cannot be traced. A number of those admitted by the Council were never
admitted by the Dean of Guild and his court ; their names are not on the
register, and consequently do not appear in the MS. Index. Occasionally a
burgess is admitted by the Guild Court by an act of Council passed some
time after! Nor was admission by the Town Council promptly followed by
that of the Guild Council—we find, for instance, W m . Lumsdain was admitted
by the Town Council 5 Sept. 1744—and only six years later, 12 Oct. 1750, did
the Guild Council admit him. John Russel, writer to the signet, admitted by
the Town Council 5 Aug. 1741, became B. and G. only on 15 Sept. 1749, after
eight years' delay, while Dr. Robert Hay waited for nearly ten years, from
28 May 1740 to 10 Jan. 1750, ere he became a "freeman."
    But the apprentices were far'more dilatory.
        Robert Thomson, skinner, entered p. 18 July 1711, burgess 18 Feb.
            1747-
        John Somervail, wright, entered p. 3 Mar. 1797, burgess 11 Feb. 1736.
        Robert Young, wright, entered p. 25 Oct. 1682, burgess 19 Sept. 1722.
        Robert Tod, wright, entered p. 18 July and 22 Aug. 1705, burgess
           7 Mar. 1750.
    Evidently there was no advantage to be gained by early admission.
    The same may be noticed in the case of guild brethren, entering sometimes
long after admission as burgesses.
    It is quite evident that despite all the care taken in entering apprentices,
burgesses and guild brethren, omissions have occurred.           We find men
admitted burgesses as apprentices who are not entered in the apprentice roll ;
or others entered by right of a father burgess, whom we seek in vain in the
 burgess roll.
    Occasionally the Council passed a second act admitting some one as B.
and G , apparently forgetting that this had been done already.
    Admission as a burgess and guild brother without payment of dues—
"gratis"—was in many cases purely complimentary, and conferred no rights
or privileges, unless particularly specified.
    In some cases it was granted " f o r good service done," such as the ad-
 mission of Wm. Blair, gratis, " f o r good service done at the late fire in the
 head of the West Bow (29 Sept. 1710)
    In at least one case the widow of a burgess and guild brother seems to
have conferred the right of admission on her second husband. See Thomas
 Espline, 30 Aug. 1710.
   Note.—The form of the entry in the Minutes of Town Council differs
      occasionally so far from that in the Burgess Roll as to make it worth
      while to note both. Where no " r i g h t of admission " is mentioned, the
      admission is by payment as exigible from an "unfreeman."
   The paucity of cutlers within the city may be gauged by the entry of
Robert Boog, 26 Apr. 1748, when there was " n o quorum of their craft within
the city," and the Town Council had to assume the responsibility.
   Chairmasters seem to have been admitted invariably on payment of the
dues as unfreemen. They served no apprenticeship, and, curiously enough,
seem to have had no right by parentage or marriage.
    19 Mar. 1701.—Act discharging unfree traders to keep shops, cellars, etc.
for selling wares, drink ; also prohibiting burgesses to keep more shops or
cellars than one, contrary to law ; offenders' shops to be shut and themselves
amerciat at the discretion of Dean of Gild and Council.

    9 Jan. 1705.—" Patrick Wilkie and Archibald Hamilton, merchants in
Leith, be thir presents binds and oblidges them and each of them while they
live or reseid in Leith that they shall not hereafter deall in forraigne trade
under the penalty of fyve hundred merks Scots to be payde be each of them in
caise of failyie attour being oblidged imediately thereafter to come and reseid
at Edr."
    28 Sept. 1705.—The Dean of Gild and his Council grants libertie and
licence to Mrs. Marie Edwards and Mrs. Alice Murray, housekeeper to the
Dutches douger of Argyle, to keep publiek shops within the citie and to sell
therein all maner of merchant ware in use to be sold be burgeses and gild
brethren, and that during their being unmarried, conforme to an act of Councill
of the dait of thir presents."
    Note.—6 Sept. 1706.—John Jeffrey, combmaker, allowed to trade and
merchandise within the good town all the days of his life.
    7 Jan. 1708.—"The Councill grants liberty and licence to Alexr. Pringle,
flesher, and his spouse to trade during all the days of their life as an (sic)
burges, and that for payment of three pound sterling."
    8 Sept. 1708.—" The same day the Councill authorised and appointed John
Mirrie, present deacon conveener, to sell an burges and guild brother ticket
to the best advantage to any person he thinks fitt. The price whereof to be
applied by him for the behooff of the Trads Maiden Hospitall, and the Councill
declared the person's admission to be as valid and effectual to him as if he had
payed the same composition to the Dean of Guild."
    22 Sept. 1708.—"Richard Watkins, merchant, compeiring is mad burges
of this burgh and gave his oath, etc. and payed to the Dean of Gild fourty
two pounds scottis money in satisfaction of the dewes conforme to ane act of
the toun council of the date of thir presents."

     9 J f y '752.—Benjamin Ramage, p. to Adam Watkins, H . M . Printer and
Stationer for Scotland, B. In the privately printed " Reminiscences " (p. xxxv)
of Charles Cowan of Logan House, ex-M.P., speaking of the paper mills at
Valleyfield, Penicuick, he says, " they were occasionally possessed and wrought
by the King's printer of the day. There is a tradition in the parish that a
King's printer, named Watkins, about the middle of last (i.e. 18th) century met
with a very appalling death. He had been a very godless man, and one
Sunday he had been walking with a friend towards Pennicuick House during
the hours of divine service, when a storm of thunder and lightning suddenly
set in ; he blasphemously defied the power of the Almighty, and was immed-
iately struck down dead. I t created a great sensation in the congregation,
who were informed of the death by the officiating minister before the close of
the service."
   4 May 1709.—Chamberlain appointed to pay to Mr. John James Caesar, an
German minister Calvinist and of the Presbyterian persuasion, the sum of
twenty pound sterling for a help to the upholding of the German congregation
and meeting of the said persuasion at London.
    10 A u g . 1709.—"The Councill granted liberty and licence to Sarah
Dalrymple, daughter to Charles Dalrymple of Waterside, to use her trade of
japanning as a burges of this city all the days of her lifetime and her con-
tinuing unmarried. Providing always she imploy the freemen of this city for
the timber work."

    21 Nov. I 7 i l . - T h e Dean of Guild represented to the Council that in
obedience to their appointment, 7 Feb. last, he caused call for I nomas Vint
and James M'Culloch their burgess tickets, and also caused close up their chop
doors and mark the recalling of their admissions in the Dean of Gild Books.
But since the said Thomas Vint has at his own hand without any licence either
of the Council or Dean of Gild Court opened his chop and exercised his
employment as formerly, upon which the said Dean of Gild caused close up
his chop of new again. Upon which the said Thomas Vint has raised
summonds of reduction and improbation and by vertue thereof caused sumond
the said Dean of Gild to compear before the Lord of Council and Session and
therefore the Dean of Guild desired the Council might stand by and defend
him in what he had done, in the said matter by their appointment. The
Council approved of the Dean of Gild's procedure, and appointed their lawyers
and agent to be employed to defend him upon the Town's expenses.
   28 A p r . 1712.—The Merchant Company complain of evils arising from false
and improper designations given to persons admitted as burgesses and guild
brethern. The Council ordain that no one be admitted until his claim be
openly read and approved by Dean of Guild and his Council, and that his
particular business be designed in his burges ticket, and a full record
kept.
   25 June 1712—(George Bailie.)—The Maiden Hospital was in 1695 founded
by the craftsmen of Edinburgh and Mary Erskine, relict of James Hair,
druggist, burgess of Edinburgh, she being "the first who projected and
destinated funds for Maiden Hospitals in the City of Edinburgh." She
accordingly bears the Title of the Founder of the Hospital, and it is provided
that two of the name of Erskine shall be for ever governours thereof, named in
the first instance by herself-these two being (probably as relatives) the
notorious Master James Erskin of Grange, Senator of the College of Justice,
who marooned his mad wife in St. Kilda, and Master David Erskine, advocate.
The governors, by grant from the Town Council, enjoyed the right of nominat-
ing one man annually for admission as a burgess gratis.
   29 A u g . 1712.—Master of the Merchant Company authorised to sell one
burgess and guild brother ticket, the price to be applied for the behoof of the
Merchants and Mary Arskin their Maiden Hospital.

guild brother ticket.

    4 Nov. 1713.—"John Kay, workman in weigh-house, judicially being accused
for buying with a large weight and selling by a lesser, acknowledged the same.
Wherefore the Dean of Gild and Councill fynes in twenty shilling sterling and
he present oblidges himself to pay the same on demand and that he shall never
committ the like in tyme coming directly or indirectly under the pain of fourty
pounds Scotts. Declares he cannot wryte." (A scrawl seems to indicate an
attempt at a guided signature.)
   10 June 1715.—The Master and also the Convener of the Merchant Com-
pany each allowed to sell one B. and G. ticket.

   16 Oct. 1717.—"Grissell Pillans is impowered to trade within the citty as ane
burges and gild brother thereof dureing her single lyfe and virginity for pay-
ment of ane hundered merkes Scotts money conforme to ane act of Councill of
the date of their presents, and the Court declare that in case she shall marry
ane husband who hes not right to enter burges and gild brother other ways then
by composition that this composition shall be imputed in part payment thereof."
   The same day Margaret Nash is admitted on the same footing, "she
behaving herself as becomes, and paying taxes and bearing burdens with the
other burgesses and gild brethren."

   29 Nov 1717— " I t being moved that Isaac Queen being a Jew was
uncapable of being invested with the right of burgess and gild brother and to
enjoy the priviledges consequentiall thereto, yet that for the benefit of the touiie
he paying a hundered pound he might be endowed dureing his life with the
priviledge of useing and exerciseing any trade merchandise or employment
within this city and libertys thereof, and he being present and payd the sd
hundered pound the motion was approved of and that priviledge granted
accordingly."
    16 Oct. 1717.—Walter Kyll or Kyle, m t , who entered 'prentice 19 Oct 1616,
made B. and G. on his paying so much in respect of his setting up a shop before
the expiry of his indentures.
    16 M y 1718.—In consequence of a petition given in by the maltmen and
brewers of Leith against unfreemen who have taken up the trade of brewing
in Leith, underselling the legitimate brewers, and encouraging smuggling and
hidden trade, the Town Council discharge all persons other than burgesses of
Edinburgh and incorporate maltsters of Leith to take up or carry on the trade
of brewing in Leith, under pain of one hundred merks Scots. A number ot
unfree brewers in Leith entered, burgesses of Edinburgh accordingly.
     10 Sept. 1718.-^200 Scots paid to Treasurer of the Merchant Maidens
Hospital, and /100 Scots to the deacon convener of Trades, in lieu of com-
pliment of disposal of two and one burgess tickets respectively, as was the
custom formerly.
      17 Sept. 1718.—The Council ordains that the Lord Provost, four bailies,
Dean of Guild and Treasurer wear black velvet coats as a garb of distinction
during their office, and that the sum of ten pounds stg. be paid to each of the
four bailies, Dean of Guild and Treasurer before their quitting office in place
of the burgess tickets formerly given them and of the one hundred pounds
Scots which has been paid to them lately in lieu of these tickets, upon condition

       22 J u l y 1719.—John Law, Lord and Earl of Tankerville. This is not the
 Tankerville family of Bennet, at Chillingham, but its namesake in France on
  the river Seine.
       In "Les Ecossais en France" (Francisque-Michel), 1862, Vol. I I , p. 4^3,
  speaking of this famous John Law, the author states that the Laws of Lauriston are
  not the direct descendants of the financier. " Cette famille est issue du fiére de
  l'inventeur du système, qui l'avait rejoint en France et fut compris avec lul.
  La Duchesse de Bourbon fit placer les deux neveux de John Law au service
  dans les Indes orientales. L'ainè, Jacques Francois Law, comte de Tancarville,
  devint chevalier de Saint Louis, etc." He adds a note on "Tancarville : -
  "Cette terre venait, a ce qu.il parait, de John Law. Dangeau ecnt dans son
  Journal, a la date du 31 aoüt 1718. ' O n dit que le comte d'Evreux a vendu la
   terre de Tancarville a M . Law, qui lui en donne 650,000 livres et une pension
   viagère de 6000 francs.' "                                                       .

     25 Sept. 1730.—"The Council with the Extraordinar Deacons considering it

     2 June 173J.—The Council considering the act of Council of 24 Dec. 1703
 limiting the import of gratis burgess tickets to a term of five years, and
 considering that there is no distinction made in the tenor of gratis tickets that
 are given to such as are servants to H . M . Commissioners to the General
 Assembly, and to such like, from the honorary tickets that are given to noblemen
 and gentlemen in compliment, do ordain that hereafter in all gratis tickets
 which are not given in compliments to noblemen and gentlemen, that there
 shall be an explicit reference to the said act of Council, limiting the term for
 which the freedom is thereby intended, and appoints the gratis tickets granted
 26 May to the Earl of Loudon's servants to be made out after that tenor.
    l o j u n e 1731.—Formula of gratis burgess ticket:—" Edinburgh, the

     i A p r . 1747.—"The same day His Royal Highness William Augustus,
 Duke of Cumberland, Brunswick, Lunenburgh, etc, etc. Captain General of
all His Majestie's land forces and Commander in Chief of the allyed army,
etc, etc, etc, was by the Right Honble. George Drummond, E s q , Lord
 Provost of the City of Edinburgh, Robert Montgomery, William Hamilton,
John Brown and Andrew Wardrop, baillies of the said city, Thomas Allan,
Dean of Gild, and the Gild Councill, and hereby is invested with the freedom
of this city as a testimony of their grateful sense of the glorious services done
by his Royal Highness to his Sacred Majesty and the British Nation in
happily crushing the late detestable Rebellion, giving a total overthrow to the
rebells in the memorable Battell of Culloden, restoring the publiek tranquillity,
makeing way for the free exercise of goverment in this city, secureing the
trade liberties and laws of Great Britain, and transmitting to posterity along
with the immortal honours of a young hero the invaluable blessings enjoyed
under the auspicious reigns of the Protestant Princes of the illustrious House
of Hanover,— conform to an act of the Town Council of the date the 3rd day
of January last, 1747, and the seal of the city affixt."

    20 Nov. 1751.—"Mr. Sands, City Treasurer, represented that the indentures
entered into with James M'Crabie as ane apprentice with the city's casswav
layers being now expired, and as the overseer of the city's publiek works
informs that M'Crabie is pretty much master of his business and that the toun
will have occasion for his service farther. That James Pirrie, son to lames
Pirrie, a souldier in the garrison of Edinbr. Castle, was willing to enter into
indentures on the like termes with M'Crabie, whereforthe Treasurer desired the
Council s directions in what is above represented. Which being considered
 hey ordered the treasurer to give M'Crabie a declaration with respect to his
haveing faithfully served the city during the years of his indentures upon
Al Cables acknowledging that he is fully satisfied and paid of his wages
Also they agreed to continue M'Crabie in the city's service as a casswaylayer
and to give him the ordinary wages during the Council's pleasure. And they
authorised the Treasurer to enter into indentures in behalf of the city with the
said James Pirrie on the like conditions with M'Crabie."

      18 June 1755—"Mr. David Flint, old Dean of Gild, represented he was
  well informed that Richard Beckford, esquire, Member of Parliament for the
  City ot Bristol had been generously pleased to signify that he was to give two
  Hundred pounds Jamaica currency annually for the four ensuing years in order
 to promote the exportation of linnen made in Scotland from the Port of Leith
  1 herefore moved the Councill that they would be pleased as a mark of their
 gratitude for this singular favour to the country and to the City of Edinburgh
 in particular to order a burges ticket, for Mr. Beckford, and to recommend to
  he city s member when he goes next to Parliament to deliver it himself with
                u n           n       5
 \T y° "          best compliments. Which having been considered by the
 Magistrates and Council, they appointed the Dean of Gild and his Councill to
 admit and receive the said Richard Beckford a burges and gild brother of this
 city, dispensing with the Dues for the good services done by him to the interest
 thereof. Whereanent these presents shall be a warrant."

I N this volume is contained the Roll or Register

of Burgesses and Guild-brethren of the City of

Edinburgh from 1st January 1761 to 31st Decem-

ber 1841.

   Some notes, etc, will be found at the beginning

and end of the volume.

178                 Roll of Edinburgh              Burgesses.             [1761-1841


Exchange belonging to Robert Thomson, merchant, and thereafter had
absconded. Upon which they had advertised a Reward of Ten Guineas to be
paid by the City Treasurer to any person who should apprehend the said
James Ireland and upon his being convicted. The Council approved of the
procedure of the Magistrates in the said matter.
    It was at the same time represented that the Magistrates had got informa-
tion that the said James Ireland had made his escape to Newcastle, whereupon
the Lord Provost had wrote to the Lord Mayor of that place desiring that he
might take the trouble to cause search to be made there for him, and that the
Mayor of Newcastle had caused apprehend him after a pursuit of fourty miles
in which that gentleman had been at great pains as well as in many other
matters relating to the Interest of this City, and therefore it was moved that
the freedom of the city should be conferred on him for his good services and
that the Lord Provost should acquaint him thereof and at the same time desire
of him to pay the officer who apprehended Ireland in such manner as he
should judge reasonable, which afterwards would be repaid to him by the
City Treasurer."

    19 Dec. 1764.—"It being represented by the Dean of Gild that an Index
of Honorary Burgesses would be very necessary and convenient and moved
that the same should be done and the Dean of Gild clerk authorised for that
purpose, D i d therefore authorize Mr. Alves to make out the foresaid Index
commencing from Michaelmas one thousand seven hundered and fourty two
and to be executed betwixt and the first day of March next."
    7 Au%. 1765.—"Alexr. Newlands, mt., compearing, is made B. of this city
in r. of Alexr. Newlands, m t , B., his father, and he paid his dues, gave his
oath, &c. Thereafter it having been represented to the Dean of Guild and
his Council that the aforesaid Alexr. Newlands, m t , was only the natural son
of Alexr. Newlands, m t , and consequently had no right, the Court Rescinds
the above entry and Discharge the Clerk of Court from giving out the Ticket."
[There is accordingly no entry on the margin of dues paid.]
   June 1766.—The     Lord Provost signes James       Stuart.
   12 Nov. 1766.—Sir William Forbes, Barronet, compearing, is made Burges
and Gildbrother of this City as having served an apprenticeship to Messrs.
Coutts Brothers & Co, merchants, Burgesses & Gildbretheren thereof, and
he paid the usual fees of recording his Indentures and admission money &

   8 Oct. 1766.—Sir Wm. Forbes, Barronet, compearing is entered an apprentice
to Messrs. Couts Brothers & C o , merts, Burges & Gildbrethren for five years.

    % A p r . 1767.—Josiah Corthine, E s q , collector of H . M . Customs at H u l l ;
William Hildyard, Esq., in Great Grimsby, Lincolnshire; and Archd. Douglas
at Exmouth, Devonshire, admitted "burgesses and gildbrethren of this city
in the most ample form for the good services done by them to the Interest
thereof by their humane Conduct in saving a great property belonging to the
citizens when the ship ' Betsey ' was stranded on the Lincolnshire coast."

    13 May 1767.—" Considering that a practice has for some time prevail'd of
giving the freedom of the city to many persons indiscriminately which has
been attended with great Inconvenience, The Council Do therefore Enact &
Declare that no Burges Ticket shall be granted in time comeing to any person
whomever, but such as are invested with public character or shall have
signalized himself in the service of his countrey or this city."
    29 J u l y 1767.—Letter from Mr. George Chalmers, mert. in E d i n r , addressed
to the Lord Provost, stating that the present Postmaster-General, the Earl of
Hilsborough and Lord Despencer had agreed to order the mail to and from
London to pass by the direct course between Ferrybridge and Northallerton
without making the circuit of York, alteration to take effect on 10th Oct. next,

    30 August 1775.—"Appoint the Dean of Gild and his Council to admit and
receive Burgesand Gildbrother of this City in the most ample form Sir Grey
Cooper secretary to the right Honble. the Board of Treasury descended from
the ancient Family of Cooper of Gogar in this County whose ancestor Simon
Cooper appears upon Record to have been a great Baron in the year 1296—
and whose other ancestor Sir John Cooper the First Baronet of the Family
represented the County of Edinr. in the Scots Parliamt. for many years was
one of the Commissioners of the Kingdom at the Treaty of Rippon (sic), and in
other High Stations distinguished himself in the management of public affairs,
in consideration of the Family he represents and of his services to the Nation."
    23 Oct. 1776.—A petition was presented for James Whitit setting forth that
on the Eleventh of October last he was admitted a burges of the City In right
of Elizabeth Muirhead his wife the Daughter of a Freeman and paid the usual
dues of admission. That in Recording him in the Burges Book he is designed
gardner in Edinr. whereas his Proper designation is Wauker, and therefore
praying the Dean of Gild & Council would grant warrand for expeding his
Burges Ticket as a Wauker in place of a gardner. Which being considered by
the Dean of Gild and his Council They Granted warrant as Craved.
    " 10 September 1777.—The Dean of Gild and his Council Considering that
this book is much worn and some of the Leaves loose and that it is improper any
more Burgesses or Gildbrethren should be entered therein Appoint the loose
leaves to be fixed in the best manner and the book repaired Prohibite &
Discharge the Clerk of Court from entering any more Burgesses or Gild-
brethren in this book & ordain a new book to be got immediately. •
                                                      CHARLES     INNES,     D.G.''

    17 Dec. 1777.—Robert Clark, joiner.      This seems to be the first mention of

    8 J u l y 1778.—Thomas Dundas, Lieut-Col, and Major James Gordon, both
of the Royal Edinr. Volunteers, admitted B. & G. gratis, and the other Major
to be admitted likewise as soon as he shall be named by his Majesty.
   3 March 1779.—Bailie (Donald) Smith moved that as the Edinburgh
Regiment is now going abroad in the service of their country that the
Magistrates may be authorized to give the officers an Entertainment, of which
motion the Council approved and authorize accordingly.
    9 Sept. 1779.—It was represented that James Gumming, painter, was nota
Burges of this Burghand as William Milne, painter, formerly his apprentice,
has procured a Burges 'Picket and paid therefore, as deriving right thro the
said James Gumming. But upon searching the Record it really appeared That
the said James d i m m i n g never was entered Burges himself contequently the
said William Milne could not be entered as a Bulges apprentice. Therefore I
John Grieve, Esqr, Dean of Gild of the said City of Edinburgh Do hereby
Declare That the said William Milne is not a Burges of this Burgh, as set forth
111 a sederunt of the Fifth of August last and I hereby Ordain the clerks and
officer to Return him his money.

Clerks will enter no more Burgesses therein But get a New Book for that
purpose."
   3 Nov. 1790.—"Report on roup of Common Good. The Fruit Market set
to William Beaddie, Residenter at Dudingstone, at five thousand nine hundred
and forty merks yearly. Cautioners, Robert Sanderson and John Clapperton,
merchants in Edinburgh."
    12 June 1791.—"On the motion of the Lord Provost the Council admitted
Colonel Charles Graham of the forty-second Regiment of Foot, a Burges and
Guildbrother of the city, and the Lord Provost was authorised to return the
thanks of the Council to him and the other officers of that Regiment for their
attention in giving immediate assistance with large parties at several dangerous
fires which lately happened, And authorized the Magistrates to give an
entertainment to thc officers, and authorized the Lord Provost and Treasurer
to give such a small duceur as they may think proper to the Privates for their
good behaviour."

    8 Dec. 1791.—"John Wright lawfull son to Robert Wright Baker in
Haddington Served as an Apprentice to James Carfrae Merchant in Edinburgh
for the space of four years And by a Certificate on the back of the Indenture
under the hand of James Jackson & Company merchants in Edinburgh it
appears that the said John Wright served the said Company for several years
after the Expiration of the Indenture with the said James Carfrae. And
therefore the Lord Dean of Guild by his order on the back of the Indenture
appointed the same to be recorded and he thereafter admitted a Burges and
Guild Brother in Right of his Masters."

    \ Í J i l l y 1793.—" John M'Crobie merchant compearing is made Burges &
Guild Brother of this City In right of John Gibb merchant Burges & Guild
brother thereof his Master And he paid his dues and made oath in terms of
the Act of Parliament dated third day of June last respecting persons pro-
fessing the Roman Catholic Religion in Scotland."
   l A u g . 1793. —Malcom M'Naughton is admitted Guildbrother, with no
mention of his being already a burgess.
   31 A u g . 1793.—James Campbell, lint merchant, admitted Guildbrother,
with no mention of his being already a burgess.
   3' A u g . 1793.—James Wallace, bookseller, admitted burgess as 'prentice to
Francis Innes, gunsmith, burges.
    3° Sept. 1793.—George Gregory, tinplate worker, made burges in right ot
his fr. James Gregory alias M'Gregor, wigmaker.
    ii June 1795.—"In terms of a petition presented of this date, James Syme
shipmaster in Perth is hereby admitted and received a Burges of this City In
right of Chesterfield Dickson his Wife daughter of the deceased Robt. Dickson
Weaver Burges of Edinr. and the dues were paid accordingly."        (This must
have been in absentid.)
